items.title: What the Civil Service is
items.source: GOV.UK, About the Civil Service; Civil Service Code
items.body: The Civil Service is the permanent body of staff who help the government of the day develop and deliver its policies and run public services. Ministers are elected politicians and they decide policy. Civil servants advise ministers and carry out the decisions. When a new government is elected the ministers change but the civil servants stay, and they serve the new government with the same commitment. This is called political impartiality. Roughly half a million people work in the Civil Service, in many different jobs and in every part of the UK, not only in London. Most of them deliver services directly to the public, for example paying benefits, collecting tax, processing passports and running prisons and courts.

options.text: The Speaker of the House of Commons

questions.prompt: What does it mean that civil servants are politically impartial?

options.text: They may not vote in elections
They serve the government of the day whichever party is in power
They only work for the largest party
They must stay silent about all government work

questions.prompt: A general election brings in a new government. What happens to the civil servants working in a department?

options.text: They all have to reapply for their jobs
They are replaced by people chosen by the new ministers
They stay in post and serve the new government
They stop work until the new government is formed

questions.prompt: A friend asks you, a new Administrative Officer, which way the minister is leaning on a decision that has not been announced yet. What should you do?
questions.answer: Do not share it. Information about decisions that have not been announced is not yours to give out, and sharing it would break the duty of confidentiality and risk the impartiality of the Civil Service. Politely say you cannot discuss it and point them to what is already public, for example on GOV.UK. If you were unsure of the rules, ask your line manager.
questions.rubric: Should decline to share, mention confidentiality or the Civil Service Code, stay polite, and say to ask a line manager if unsure. Should not suggest hinting or giving an unofficial view.

items.title: The Civil Service Code
items.body: The Civil Service Code sets out the standards expected of every civil servant. It rests on four values: integrity (putting the obligations of public service above your own interests), honesty (being truthful and open), objectivity (basing your advice and decisions on rigorous analysis of the evidence) and impartiality (acting solely according to the merits of the case and serving equally well governments of different political persuasions). The Code is part of the terms of every civil servant's appointment. If you are asked to do something that you think is wrong, or you see something that worries you, you can raise it with your line manager or another manager first. Each department has a nominated officer you can go to in confidence. If the matter is not resolved you can take it to the independent Civil Service Commission.

questions.prompt: Which of these are the four values of the Civil Service Code?
Which of these is NOT a Civil Service value?
A manager asks you to put a figure in a report that you know is wrong. Which value is most directly at stake?
You see a colleague regularly giving priority to friends when allocating appointments. You have told your line manager once and nothing has changed. What can you do next under the Civil Service Code?
questions.answer: Keep raising it. You can go to another manager or your department's nominated officer in confidence, and if the matter is still not resolved you can bring it to the independent Civil Service Commission. Keep a note of what you saw and when, stick to facts and do not confront or gossip. Treating people fairly and on merit is part of the Code, so you are right to speak up.
questions.rubric: Should mention the nominated officer or another manager, then the Civil Service Commission as the final step. Should stress facts and notes and not gossiping or retaliation.

items.title: Departments, agencies and where the jobs are
items.source: GOV.UK, Departments, agencies and public bodies; Civil Service Jobs
items.body: The Civil Service is made up of government departments, such as the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC), the Home Office and the Ministry of Justice, and the agencies and arm's length bodies attached to them, such as the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA). Many of the largest employers, such as DWP and HMRC, have offices in towns and cities across the UK, so you may find a job close to home. The biggest group of jobs is operational delivery: people who deal directly with the public, for example processing claims, answering calls and letters, and checking cases. Other groups include policy, digital and data, finance, HR, communications and project delivery. Northern Ireland has its own Northern Ireland Civil Service. Scottish Government and Welsh Government staff are also civil servants, with their own recruitment pages.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a UK government department?
What do operational delivery roles mainly involve?

options.text: Advising the Prime Minister on policy only
Dealing directly with the public, for example processing claims, cases and enquiries

questions.prompt: Which statement about where Civil Service jobs are is most accurate?

options.text: They are in towns and cities across the UK, not only in London
They are all in central government buildings in Whitehall
They are only in Scotland and Wales

questions.prompt: You live in a small town and can only travel about 30 minutes to work because of childcare. How would you find out which Civil Service jobs might suit you?
questions.answer: Search Civil Service Jobs by location and set the distance or area to match the travel time. Create a job alert for those locations, check whether roles are advertised as part-time, flexible or hybrid, read the office location carefully in each advert, and check the contact details in the advert to ask any question about working patterns before applying. Also look at the websites of nearby departments that run local offices and contact centres.
questions.rubric: Should mention searching Civil Service Jobs by location, job alerts, reading the advert for location and working pattern, and asking the contact named in the advert. Should show practical planning around childcare.

items.title: Grades and where most people start
items.source: GOV.UK, Civil Service grades; Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Civil Service jobs are organised into grades. From the bottom they run: Administrative Assistant (AA), Administrative Officer (AO), Executive Officer (EO), Higher Executive Officer (HEO), Senior Executive Officer (SEO), Grade 7, Grade 6 and then the Senior Civil Service. Pay and exact titles vary between departments and by location, and each advert states its own salary. Most people who join without a Civil Service background start at AA or AO. Many AA and AO adverts do not ask for formal qualifications. They test your skills through the application, tests and interview instead. EO roles carry more responsibility, for example looking after a small team or a more complex caseload. Moving up is normal: people often apply for the next grade after a year or two once they have shown they can do the work.

questions.prompt: Which of these grades is a typical starting grade for someone new to the Civil Service?
Which list puts the grades in order from lowest to highest?
An AO job advert says no formal qualifications are required. What does that most likely mean?

options.text: Anyone who applies will get an interview
You will not need to take any tests
You are assessed on your skills and how you perform in the selection process, not on certificates

questions.prompt: You have been out of paid work for eight years raising children. Should you aim first for an AO or an EO role? Explain your thinking.
questions.answer: Aim first for AA or AO roles. They are designed as entry points, often need no formal qualifications and fit a person whose evidence comes from unpaid work. Use experience such as running a household, volunteering and caring as evidence of the skills asked for. After a year or two of showing you can do the work you can apply for EO roles, which expect more independence and often some experience of supervising or complex work. It is possible to apply for EO sooner if the advert's criteria match your evidence, but it is a bigger step.
questions.rubric: Should recommend starting at AA/AO, explain the reasons, mention using unpaid experience as evidence, and mention a later move to EO. Should be realistic, not dismissive of aiming higher.
